structure.title: Robert Lawrence Kuhn: Closer To Truth · Kuhn keeps the first conversations short
structure.text: Robert Lawrence Kuhn can spend an entire exchange on what Deutsch means by a world. Just when the answer begins to make sense, Kuhn tries to restate it in his own terms. Deutsch's correction often marks the place where an everyday picture of space or time has slipped back into the question.

structure.title: Micah Redding – Logan Chipkin · Longer interviews give objections time to develop
structure.text: The format opens out with Micah Redding, John Horgan and Logan Chipkin. A question about humanity's future can lead back to what counts as an explanation. Chipkin takes the opposite route and asks what a precise idea in physics might allow someone to do with information.

structure.title: Bruce Nielson – Peter Boghossian · Several people put the same philosophy to different uses
structure.text: An economist, a computer scientist and a parent can each hear something different in the claim that people create knowledge. The later conversations range from mathematics to child-rearing. Their company matters. Bédard's discussion includes another physicist, Charles Bennett, as well as an audience able to press the speakers on what they mean.

people.name: David Deutsch
people.role: Physicist answering across several decades of conversations
people.text: Deutsch has to explain his position anew to each host. A phrase that passes without comment in one interview can take up much of another. The recordings also come from different dates, so a later formulation may give a different account of a question that seemed settled earlier in the volume.

people.name: Robert Lawrence Kuhn
people.text: Kuhn often gives Deutsch the benefit of a proposed analogy, then asks whether he has it right. The exchange gives the reader a rare opportunity to hear two people locate the exact point where their pictures of the same universe come apart.

people.name: Logan Chipkin
people.role: Editor and one of the interviewers
people.text: Chipkin assembled conversations originally addressed to separate audiences. He also appears asking about constructor theory, so the reader can see what interests the editor when he has an opportunity to put a question to Deutsch himself.

context.title: The job Deutsch gives an explanation
context.text: Two people can agree on what an instrument will register and disagree about what makes it register that way. In the interviews about quantum physics, Deutsch wants the second question pursued even when the first has an excellent answer. His dissatisfaction with a prediction alone carries over into other subjects.

context.title: A transcript holds on to the false start
context.text: Time stamps, interruptions and restatements preserve the circumstances of a remark. Reading an answer together with the next speaker's attempt to repeat it can clear up an apparent contradiction more quickly than studying the answer by itself.

passages.quote: David Deutsch’s views may have changed since the times

notice.text: Listen for the small word Kuhn hesitates to use about time.
notice.why: In one early exchange he wants to say that worlds exist at the same time and catches himself. Deutsch's reply makes time a feature to be explained within the multiverse. A hesitation lasting a few seconds exposes the difficulty better than another definition could.

passages.quote: I don’t want to say co-temporally because that may confuse everything

notice.text: Compare the questions that bring Deutsch back to computers.
notice.why: One host wants to know what the cosmos is made of. Another asks what a machine can calculate. The same vocabulary enters both answers, although establishing a limit on calculation and describing physical reality are different undertakings.

opening: David Deutsch takes the human ability to explain things seriously enough to give it consequences far beyond science. In these interviews, questions about knowledge open into arguments about computation, creativity, and what people might become capable of doing. The conversational form lets interviewers pause over claims a finished philosophical system might carry past too quickly. Across conversations recorded at different times, a reader can follow a powerful set of ideas being explained, challenged, and developed by someone willing to make unusually large claims for their reach.
